title: A doughnut stop at Congdon’s.
summary: Our Congdon’s doughnut stop in Wells, Maine, with original family photos, practical access and sensory notes, and a free printable doughnut choice board.
search: The journal / Out & about / Wells, Maine Wells, Maine · From the family camera roll A doughnut stop at Congdon’s. Sunshine, a very yellow sign, and James getting on with the doughnut. A little Maine stop, with the useful details left in. October 18, 2026 · A family field note A doughnut is not going to wait for the family photograph. Fair enough. The little storyFree choice boardAccess & sensory notesHours & ordering Some stops earn their place in the camera roll with a big view. This one has a doughnut and an enormous yellow sign. Both make a good case. Our Congdon’s photographs are full of October sunshine: the red stand, picnic tables, a blue sky, and James taking a bite while standing beside his dad. It is a small piece of our Maine trip, and exactly the sort of ordinary family moment I want to keep. The red building in these pictures is marked Congdon’s Too! There are serving windows, a little raised porch, entrance and exit signs, and picnic tables outside. James is there with his doughnut, the autumn trees behind him doing their bit for the photograph. On the Congdon’s Too! porch. The doughnut remains the main event. A bakery stop can also involve quite a few decisions. Which doughnut? Where do we order? Are we sitting here or taking it with us? Those are useful things to make clearer before everyone is standing in front of the choices. So this field note comes with something to take along: a doughnut choice board, a few communication options, and the arrival details we would want another family to have. Make the choice a little clearerA picture. A preference. Room to decide. Plain, honey dip, chocolate raised, or apple fritter? Open the picture board before you order, check what is available, and offer the choices that work for the person using it. There is room for “something else,” “no,” “more,” “help,” “break,” and “all done,” too. The board is an extra way to communicate; keep the person’s familiar AAC, gestures and other ways of responding available. Open the choice boardDownload the printable PDF The food pictures are generic illustrations, not photographs of Congdon’s products. Names follow the published doughnut menu; today’s selection may differ. The practical partThe route matters as much as the table. Here is what our photographs show, plus a few practical questions to ask before visiting. The wider view: raised porch, steps, brick paving, loose gravel and fixed-bench picnic tables. What our photographs show Steps at the standThe photographed porch has steps and railings, with entrance and exit markings. An alternate step-free route is not shown. Several surfacesThe tables in front sit on brick pavers, with loose gravel beside them and grass farther out. Check the whole route from your parking space to your destination. Picnic seatingThe visible tables have attached benches. We have not measured wheelchair clearance or confirmed an accessible table. An outdoor settingSun, shade, wind and temperature may matter to your visit. These pictures do not establish how busy or quiet the property usually is. Ordering, waiting and sensory preferences Show the choices before entering the queue and allow time to respond without repeating the question. Keep “something else” and “no” available. Match a picture to what is actually in the case before treating it as an available choice. If useful, bring familiar hearing protection and choose a place to pause before you need it. With two adults, one can collect the order while the other stays with the family member in a place that suits them. There is no requirement to turn a doughnut stop into a sit-down meal. Congdon’s online-order information lists collection at the end of the main bakery counter or at the drive-through when open. Follow your order’s pickup instructions and collect it before the bakery closes at 2 p.m. Moving a preorder to the food-truck park requires advance agreement and email confirmation from Congdon’s. Parking, bathrooms and the step-free route The After Dark FAQ describes designated accessible parking along the building and in the gravel lot, plus indoor bathrooms on the shared property. That page concerns the food-truck park; it does not verify every daytime bakery route or the photographed stand. We did not document the parking-to-door route, restroom layout, door widths or table clearance. If those details decide the visit, ask which entrance is step-free, where to park for it, and whether there is a suitable restroom and table available during your planned hours. A useful question: “We’re coming for the bakery. Which parking space and step-free entrance should we use, and can we reach the ordering counter, a table and the restroom by that route?” Contact details are below. Food ingredients, vegetarian choices and allergies Congdon’s says its house doughnuts are fried in lard. A plain doughnut therefore is not a vegetarian option. The bakery FAQ points customers avoiding animal fats toward separately packaged alternatives; confirm the individual product and availability. For allergies or dietary requirements, check the current ingredient and allergen information and ask about the exact item. A picture, flavor name or packaged alternative should not be treated as an allergen guarantee. The red stand, ice-cream signs and After Dark Our photographs show the Congdon’s Too! stand. Its separate hours and current menu were not verified. The Gifford’s sign in the pictures does not establish that ice cream was available during our stop or will be available on yours. Congdon’s After Dark is the seasonal evening food-truck park. Its website said closed for the season when checked on October 18, 2026. The bakery’s hours below should not be applied to the stand or food-truck park. A sign we photographed advertises free cornhole-board sign-out at the bar truck. Ask about current availability during the food-truck season. Main bakery · Planning informationBefore you turn onto Post Road. WhereCongdon’s Doughnuts 1090 Post Road (Route 1) Wells, Maine 04090 Open directions Bakery hours6 a.m.–2 p.m. when open. At our October 18 check: Wednesday–Monday, closed Tuesday. Days change seasonally. Check current opening days How to orderCounter/café service, with indoor dining rooms. Online pickup is also offered. Ordering & pickup options Ask about access207-646-4219 Contact Congdon’s Ask about the specific counter, route and facilities you plan to use. If one particular doughnut is the planUse Congdon’s advance-order option by 5 p.m. the day before to reserve the chosen flavors. Same-day online orders depend on remaining stock. Choose an open pickup day and follow the collection instructions. title: A short plan you can actually use.
summary: Three fill-in tools for an ordinary week: a leaving-the-house card, a one-good-thing day plan and a household handoff. Fill them here, copy them or print a blank set.
search: Use it · Copy & printA short plan you can actually use.Three fill-in tools for an ordinary week: a leaving-the-house card, a one-good-thing day plan and a household handoff. Fill them here, copy them or print a blank set.In this guideStart with one card for one recurring moment.Tool 1: the leaving-the-house card.Tool 2: one good thing, with room around it.Tool 3: hand over one complete household job.The ten-minute weekly reset.Start with one card for one recurring moment.Pick the transition that regularly creates the most searching: leaving for the pool, getting out for an appointment, or working out dinner. Write down what would actually make that moment easier. A planning card can hold the short list so nobody has to recreate it each time.Keep a familiar communication system in place. A website worksheet is not a replacement for someone's communication tools or support plan. Words, an existing symbol system, actual objects or photographs may work better for different people. Use the form that is already meaningful, with a respectful tone and a real way to decline or change the plan.The tools below run in this page. They do not submit or save your entries to a server, and there is no account. Refreshing or leaving can clear your work. Copy or print anything you want to keep. Leave out names, addresses, personal care details, medical information and other private records, especially on a shared device or a sheet left in public view.Tool 1: the leaving-the-house card.Write only the things somebody needs to act on before leaving. “Pool bag by the door” is easier to use than “be organized.” Keep the everyday bag and a small last-minute list separate so you do not repack everything.Before we leaveThe one destinationTime to leaveAlready readyAdd at the last minuteOne detail to confirmIf plans changeCopy this cardPrint this cardClear entriesPlace a paper version where the packing happens. If it needs to be carried, fold it into the bag's dry pouch. Review the list after two or three uses and remove anything that nobody needs to see.Tool 2: one good thing, with room around it.Plan the part people are actually looking forward to first. Add the arrival, a break and the way home. Keep optional extras genuinely optional. Example: aquarium visit, familiar lunch, home; a second shop remains a possibility rather than a requirement.A day that fitsThe good partFirstNextA place or way to pauseThe shorter versionHow we finishCopy this cardPrint this cardClear entriesOffer choices that are possible that day. Allow time to respond in the person's usual way. A request for a break or an early finish should have a practical response, rather than appearing on paper without a way to use it.Tool 3: hand over one complete household job.A useful handoff says what, when and what “finished” looks like. It reduces the follow-up questions without turning the household into a project-management app. Keep private care handovers in their existing appropriate channels.One complete jobThe jobWhen it needs doingMaterials live hereFinished meansCopy this cardPrint this cardClear entriesAgree on the handoff with the person doing the job. A card does not assign responsibility by itself. For shared tasks, separate the useful pieces: one person chooses the meal, another gets the pan, another clears the table, with the ordinary help each person needs.The ten-minute weekly reset.Two minutes: check the calendar you already use. Pick the two or three plans that affect meals, transport or packing.Three minutes: choose a familiar easy meal for the busiest evening and check the ingredients.Two minutes: replenish one recurring kit, such as the swim bag or gift drawer. Add only what ran out.Two minutes: agree on one household handoff. Check the person has the time, information and materials.One minute: remove an outdated note. Decide which one card needs to be visible this week.Try the smallest version for a week. If the card becomes another thing to maintain, shorten it. Make the available options understandable, using the person’s familiar communication and support. A person may want company, help with one part, time nearby or space on their own. The NJC Communication Bill of Rights affirms that people should be addressed directly, have meaningful choices and be able to express refusal. Keep those possibilities visible in the plan.
